q.intro.text: Five friends, Ana, Ben, Cy, Dev and Eli, run a club. They need a three-person committee to plan the spring trip. No titles: the three just serve on it. How many different committees are possible? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps on the same five friends. Press each one. The picture moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Pretend the three get roles: president, vice president, secretary. Five choices for president, then four left, then three. Five times four times three is sixty ordered slates, like Ben, Dev, Ana.

e.step1.text: Here are all sixty slates, sorted. Each row holds the six slates made from the same three friends. Ten rows of six.

e.step2.text: Swap test. A B C and B C A are different slates, but the same committee. Three people can be ordered in three factorial ways: three times two times one, which is six. So every committee is counted exactly six times.

e.step3.text: So divide by three factorial, not by three. Sixty divided by six is ten committees. That is C of five, three: the ordered count over the r factorial orders of each group.

e.why.text: Quick check: why divide the sixty by six?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. Each group of three appears once for each of its six orders, so dividing by six counts it once.

e.why.byr.text: Three people make six orders, not three: A B C, A C B, B A C, B C A, C A B, C B A. Divide by three factorial, which is six.

e.why.order.text: How they are picked does not matter. The committee has no roles, so A B C and C B A are the same committee.

t.intro.text: Seven runners race in the four hundred meter final. The top three get gold, silver and bronze, and the same top three go on to the state meet. The first step is done for you.

t.pod.text: How many different podiums, gold, silver and bronze, are possible?

t.pod.keep.text: Three hundred forty-three is seven times seven times seven. A runner cannot win two medals. One fewer runner for each next medal.

t.pod.nr.text: Twenty-one is seven times three. Multiply the choices for each medal: seven, then six, then five.

t.pod.no.text: Multiply the three slots: seven times six times five.

t.pod.ok.text: Yes. Seven times six times five is two hundred ten podiums.

t.ord.text: Take one trio, say Ana, Ben and Cy. In how many orders can they fill the podium?

t.ord.three.text: Three people, but more orders: three choices for gold, then two for silver, then one. Three times two times one.

t.ord.no.text: Three choices for gold, two for silver, one for bronze.

t.ord.ok.text: Yes. Three factorial, three times two times one, is six orders of the same trio.

t.trio.text: How many different trios can go on to the state meet, with no order?

t.trio.orders.text: Two hundred ten counts every trio six times, once per podium order. Going to state has no order.

t.trio.three.text: Seventy divides by three. Each trio appears in three factorial, which is six, podiums. Divide by six.

t.trio.no.text: Each trio appears in six podiums. Divide two hundred ten by six.

t.trio.ok.text: Yes. Two hundred ten divided by six is thirty-five trios. That is C of seven, three.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked ten committees, and you were right: sixty ordered slates, each committee six times.

q.cb.orders.text: At the start you picked sixty. That counts every committee six times, once per order. Without roles, sixty divided by six is ten.

q.cb.byr.text: At the start you picked twenty: sixty divided by three. Three people have six orders, not three, so it is sixty divided by six, which is ten.

q.cb.none.text: Unordered groups: count the ordered ways, then divide by the r factorial orders of each group.

p.intro.text: A basketball team has seven players. Five start the game and two sit on the bench. Jo says: there are more ways to choose the five starters than the two on the bench, because five is more than two. Is Jo right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.no.larger.text: Choosing five starters also chooses the two who sit. Every choice of one side is a choice of the other.

p.no.luck.text: It is no accident. The match between starters and bench works for any team size.

p.no.examples.text: Three examples do not prove it for all twenty-one. The reason has to cover every line-up.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.c1.text: Right. Watch three starting fives: each one leaves its own pair on the bench.

p.c2.text: Right. Read the list from the left: the bench pair decides the five.

p.c3.text: Right. Twenty-one bench pairs, so twenty-one starting fives.

p.done.text: That's a proof. Choosing the r to take is the same as choosing the n minus r to leave. C of n, r equals C of n, n minus r, for every n and r.
